Received 1990 January 25; in original form 1989 September 20 SUMMARY The Foyers Sandstone, a constituent of the Old Red Sandstone of northern Scotland, located on the eastern flank of the Great Glen Fault, has yielded a multicomponent palaeomagnetic structure. The principal magnetization (called the B component), with in situ mean direction D, I = 185", +8"; ag5 = 2.7", post-dates the local 'mid'-Devonian (Acadian) tectonic event, but this direction corresponds well with characteristic directions displayed by Devonian and Lower Carboniferous rocks of Scotland. The most significant overprinted component, the A2 magnetiza- tion, with in situ mean direction D, I = 194", -27"; ag5 = 4. lo, has a more patchy occurrence than the B remanence, the strongest development of A2 being observed at sites that are situated close to the Great Glen Fault zone. The A2 direction is consistent with a Hercynian age. A third magnetization, the A1 component, of suggested Lower Tertiary age, has been found at one of the sites close to the fault zone. The A2 and B remanences support previously proposed declination discor- dances in corresponding magnetizations across the Great Glen Fault. It is concluded that the Foyers Sandstone developed its multicomponent magnetization through repeated tectonic events on the Great Glen Fault in Acadian, Hercynian and Alpine times respectively. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: he sedimentary complex, and as a precaution against unrecognized anisotropy effects caused by any superimposed structural fabric, measurements of anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) were carried out on five specimens from each of the 10 principal palaeomagnetic sites. The measurements show relatively low anisotropies, varying between 1.8 and 9 per cent (average 4.3), and the AMS data give mostly well-defined oblate magnetic ellipsoids (Fig. 8). With two exceptions, sites 3 and 15, the magnetic foliation plane is oriented very close to the measured bedding plane, suggesting that the AMS results arc principally governed by a primary bedding-oriented fabric. The maximum susceptibility (Kma,.) varies both within and between the sites, but the two directional populations that dominate the Foyers ORS, components B and A2, show consistent groupings (see also Fig. 9 for B-component site mean distribution). Hence, we cannot infer any noticeable relationship between the palaeomag- netic directions and the AMS structure. 4 INTERPRETATION; TECTONOMAGNETIC ASPECTS As outlined above the Foyers Sandstone has a multicom- ponent palaeomagnetic structure, but splitting the mag- netization into its components has been effectively accomplished by thermal demagnetization. Received 1990 January 25; in original form 1989 September 20 SUMMARY The Foyers Sandstone, a constituent of the Old Red Sandstone of northern Scotland, located on the eastern flank of the Great Glen Fault, has yielded a multicomponent palaeomagnetic structure. The principal magnetization (called the B component), with in situ mean direction D, I = 185", +8"; ag5 = 2.7", post-dates the local 'mid'-Devonian (Acadian) tectonic event, but this direction corresponds well with characteristic directions displayed by Devonian and Lower Carboniferous rocks of Scotland. The most significant overprinted component, the A2 magnetiza- tion, with in situ mean direction D, I = 194", -27"; ag5 = 4. lo, has a more patchy occurrence than the B remanence, the strongest development of A2 being observed at sites that are situated close to the Great Glen Fault zone. The A2 direction is consistent with a Hercynian age. A third magnetization, the A1 component, of suggested Lower Tertiary age, has been found at one of the sites close to the fault zone. The A2 and B remanences support previously proposed declination discor- dances in corresponding magnetizations across the Great Glen Fault. It is concluded that the Foyers Sandstone developed its multicomponent magnetization through repeated tectonic events on the Great Glen Fault in Acadian, Hercynian and Alpine times respectively. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: he sedimentary complex, and as a precaution against unrecognized anisotropy effects caused by any superimposed structural fabric, measurements of anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) were carried out on five specimens from each of the 10 principal palaeomagnetic sites. The measurements show relatively low anisotropies, varying between 1.8 and 9 per cent (average 4.3), and the AMS data give mostly well-defined oblate magnetic ellipsoids (Fig. 8). With two exceptions, sites 3 and 15, the magnetic foliation plane is oriented very close to the measured bedding plane, suggesting that the AMS results arc principally governed by a primary bedding-oriented fabric. The maximum susceptibility (Kma,.) varies both within and between the sites, but the two directional populations that dominate the Foyers ORS, components B and A2, show consistent groupings (see also Fig. 9 for B-component site mean distribution). Hence, we cannot infer any noticeable relationship between the palaeomag- netic directions and the AMS structure. 4 INTERPRETATION; TECTONOMAGNETIC ASPECTS As outlined above the Foyers Sandstone has a multicom- ponent palaeomagnetic structure, but splitting the mag- netization into its components has been effectively accomplished by thermal demagnetization. Received 1990 January 25; in original form 1989 September 20 SUMMARY The Foyers Sandstone, a constituent of the Old Red Sandstone of northern Scotland, located on the eastern flank of the Great Glen Fault, has yielded a multicomponent palaeomagnetic structure. The principal magnetization (called the B component), with in situ mean direction D, I = 185", +8"; ag5 = 2.7", post-dates the local 'mid'-Devonian (Acadian) tectonic event, but this direction corresponds well with characteristic directions displayed by Devonian and Lower Carboniferous rocks of Scotland. The most significant overprinted component, the A2 magnetiza- tion, with in situ mean direction D, I = 194", -27"; ag5 = 4. lo, has a more patchy occurrence than the B remanence, the strongest development of A2 being observed at sites that are situated close to the Great Glen Fault zone. The A2 direction is consistent with a Hercynian age. A third magnetization, the A1 component, of suggested Lower Tertiary age, has been found at one of the sites close to the fault zone. The A2 and B remanences support previously proposed declination discor- dances in corresponding magnetizations across the Great Glen Fault. It is concluded that the Foyers Sandstone developed its multicomponent magnetization through repeated tectonic events on the Great Glen Fault in Acadian, Hercynian and Alpine times respectively. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: he sedimentary complex, and as a precaution against unrecognized anisotropy effects caused by any superimposed structural fabric, measurements of anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) were carried out on five specimens from each of the 10 principal palaeomagnetic sites. The measurements show relatively low anisotropies, varying between 1.8 and 9 per cent (average 4.3), and the AMS data give mostly well-defined oblate magnetic ellipsoids (Fig. 8). With two exceptions, sites 3 and 15, the magnetic foliation plane is oriented very close to the measured bedding plane, suggesting that the AMS results arc principally governed by a primary bedding-oriented fabric. The maximum susceptibility (Kma,.) varies both within and between the sites, but the two directional populations that dominate the Foyers ORS, components B and A2, show consistent groupings (see also Fig. 9 for B-component site mean distribution). Hence, we cannot infer any noticeable relationship between the palaeomag- netic directions and the AMS structure. 4 INTERPRETATION; TECTONOMAGNETIC ASPECTS As outlined above the Foyers Sandstone has a multicom- ponent palaeomagnetic structure, but splitting the mag- netization into its components has been effectively accomplished by thermal demagnetization. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: magnetizations do not exhibit minimum dispersion upon proportional partial correction, which has been used to recognize synfolding magnetization. Only because we sampled widely and applied fold tests locally were we able to detect complications in the region’s history. If we had restricted our sampling to a smaller area we would have missed the initial remagnetization, and perhaps enunciated a potentially erroneous tectonic interpretation (e.g. Granirer er al. 1986). Could such a complicated history have been recognized from other data? The anomalously low within-site and between-site dispersions in this study are consistent with remagnetization but also with prolonged acquisition of original chemical remanence. The simple structure also was no help. In this regard it is worth emphasizing that present gentle attitudes of rocks, especially in convergent regions laced with thrust faults, should not be taken as proof that the rocks were always flat and unstrained. Finally, consistent polarity is no guarantee of a single magnetization. Only because we sampled widely and applied fold tests locally were we able to detect complications in the region’s history. If we had restricted our sampling to a smaller area we would have missed the initial remagnetization, and perhaps enunciated a potentially erroneous tectonic interpretation (e.g. Granirer er al. 1986). Could such a complicated history have been recognized from other data? The anomalously low within-site and between-site dispersions in this study are consistent with remagnetization but also with prolonged acquisition of original chemical remanence. The simple structure also was no help. In this regard it is worth emphasizing that present gentle attitudes of rocks, especially in convergent regions laced with thrust faults, should not be taken as proof that the rocks were always flat and unstrained. Courtillot 2, Ph. Leloup 2, Z. Yang 2, L. Xing a, J. Zhang 3, and Z. Zhuang 3 Abstract. In order to constrain better the paleogeography of the blocks that now make up China, we collected paleo- magnetic samples from Uppermost Permian to Middle Triassic limestones from two localities in the Sichuan Basin (South China Block). A low inclination component which passes both the fold test and the reversal test was found in five sites (D--46.1 ø, 1=11.9 ø, k-83.6, --8.7ø). We review corresponding remanences found in other studies of Penno- Triassic rocks from the Sichuan Basin, and show that the component is probably characteristic of the Lower Triassic. We then review paleomagnefic results from the Uppermost Permian Emeishan Basalt. Despite small local rotations, the difference between the Emeishan Basalts and the Sichuan Basin poles is interpreted to be the result of motion of the whole South China Block around the time of the Penno- Triassic boundary rather than of strain within the block. The Hornelen basin fill consists of small-scale fan deposits along the northern and southern faulted margins and a larger scale east to west axial fan-delta system. Fine-grained flood basin and lacustrine deposits associated with the axial system are situated close to the northern marginal fan bodies. Alluvium in the Hornelen basin shows a large-scale upward coarsening cyclicity (Steel et al. 1977) with smaller scale, superimposed, upward fining units. This is taken to be a response to intermittent basin subsidence and easterly depocentre migration (Steel 1976). Fine-grained flood basin and lacustrine deposits associated with the axial system are situated close to the northern marginal fan bodies. Silurian APW for Norway should coincide with that for Britain. In the literature differences between the paths have been attributed to uncertainty in their time calibration. This explanation is to some extent undermined by the fact that most of the Norwegian Devonian data lie to one side of the British APW path, not on a younger part of it. The explanation for this difference might be tectonic. Otherwise, and more probably, the two data sets might lie on a single but more complicated/tightly curved APW path than that offered here. The basins contain thick sequences of non-marine conglomerates, sandstones and siltstones in varying proportions which unconformably overlie Lower Palaeozoic metamorphic 'basement' rocks. Their age is demonstrated by Middle Devonian plant and fish remains in the youngest sandstones, and similar early Devonian fossils in the Solund basin (Kolderup 1915; Kiaer 1918; Hoeg 1936; Jarvik 1949; Steel & Aasheim 1978). Sediments within the Hornelen and Kvamshesten basins comprise a stream-flow dominated alluvial fan and fan-delta bodies, recording a sedimentary cyclicity on several scales. The Hornelen basin fill consists of small-scale fan deposits along the northern and southern faulted margins and a larger scale east to west axial fan-delta system. Fine-grained flood basin and lacustrine deposits associated with the axial system are situated close to the northern marginal fan bodies. Palaeomagnetic analysis concentrated near the basin margins has already proven itself as a powerful tool for constraining the chronology of deformation/rotation of the basinal and adjacent rocks (Torsvik et al. 1986, 1989c), yet it should be noted that thermal and chemical magnetic overprinting is likely in the rocks near to the tectonic basin margins and that further magnetotectonic information might be obtained from rocks in the interior parts of the basins. This study is a palaeomagnetic analysis of megascopically uncleaved Devonian sediments, where practical, away from the tectonic basin margins, where early/primary magnetic remanence could survive. Consequently this analysis provides additional and important, but complex, new information on the early, perhaps syn-depositional, tilting/rotation history of the sediments. The tilt corrected data from the Qiangtang Terrane at Markam (29.7"N, 98.6"E) exhibit largely clockwise deflected declinations with steep inclinations (D = 48.2", I = 49.0", a95 = 8.8"), whereas the Lhasa Terrane at Basu (3O.l0N, 96.9"E) and the Sichuan province at Ya'an (3O.l0N, 103.0"E) have northerly directions with shallow inclinations (D = -3.9", I = 23.4", a95 = 19.2" and D = 2. lo, Z = 30.7", ag5 = 11.3", respectively). The palaeomagnetic data indicate that the Qiangtang Terrane was subjected to clockwise rotation through 50" with respect to the neighbouring provinces of the Lhasa and Sichuan since the Cretaceous. Palaeomagnetic study of eastern Tibet 87 PALAEOMAGNETISM Palaeomagnetic measurements In the laboratory, individual specimens, 25 mm in diameter and 25 mm long, were prepared from each sample. Their results suggested that Stikinia had been translated northward by -1300 km as well as rotated substantially about vertical axes. This interpretation was based on the best available reference pole at that time (Irving 1979). Although, the precision of their Hazelton Group result is somewhat low, the interpretation was supported by results from the Takla Group and Axelgold intrusion (Monger & Irving 1980). re interpreted to be primary magnetizations because of the presence of two polarities and the much improved agreement of their inclinations after full tilt correction of the sites from the Bulkley Ranges. Within-locality declinations agree well; between-locality declinations are discordant. The expected cratonic declination is -340" whereas declinations from this study are 265", 227" and 328" for the Red Canyon, Zymoetz River and Telkwa Range areas respectively. These results are similar to those of Monger & Irving (1980) and we concur that the discordant declinations are the result of differential rotation about vertical axes between sample localities. Our observed mean inclination of 52" is in good agreement with Monger & Irving's (1980) result of 54". They interpreted this to indicate -1300km of northward displacement since the Early Jurassic and their interpretation was substantiated by several later studies. However, with revisions to the geologic time-scale and the Early Jurassic reference pole for North America, the Early Jurassic Canadian Cordillera palaeomagnetic data base appears latitudinally concor- dant. This indicates that Terrane I and southern Wrangellia were in much the same latitudinal position relative to the North American craton as they are now. Tect

It is therefore probable that Cretaceous Cordilleran tectonics were characterized by both regional tilting and moderate latitudinal displacement. Key words: Cordilleran tectonics, Early Jurassic, Hazelton Group palaeomagnet- ism, Telkwa Formation, Terrane I. 1 INTRODUCTION The tectonic development of the Canadian Cordillera reflects the complex evolution of a collage of allochthonous terranes. Palaeomagnetism has been useful in studying this development by providing quantitative analyses of large- scale tectonic motions within and between terranes. The first aberrant palaeomagnetic result in the western Cordillera of North America came from the Eocene Siletz River Volcanic series of Oregon (Cox 1957). However, it was not until later that Irving (1964) recognized that this aberrant result was caused by rotation about a vertical axis. Since then numerous discordant palaeomagnetic results, together with differences between Cordilleran and contiguous North American stratigraphies and differences between coeval faunas along the ancient cratonic margin, have led to the recognition that the Cordillera is a collage of terranes of different origin. This interpretation was based on the best available reference pole at that time (Irving 1979). Within-locality declinations agree well; between-locality declinations are discordant. The expected cratonic declination is -340" whereas declinations from this study are 265", 227" and 328" for the Red Canyon, Zymoetz River and Telkwa Range areas respectively. Key words: Cordilleran tectonics, Early Jurassic, Hazelton Group palaeomagnet- ism, Telkwa Formation, Terrane I. 1 INTRODUCTION The tectonic development of the Canadian Cordillera reflects the complex evolution of a collage of allochthonous terranes. Palaeomagnetism has been useful in studying this development by providing quantitative analyses of large- scale tectonic motions within and between terranes. The first aberrant palaeomagnetic result in the western Cordillera of North America came from the Eocene Siletz River Volcanic series of Oregon (Cox 1957). However, it was not until later that Irving (1964) recognized that this aberrant result was caused by rotation about a vertical axis. Since then numerous discordant palaeomagnetic results, together with differences between Cordilleran and contiguous North American stratigraphies and differences between coeval faunas along the ancient cratonic margin, have led to the recognition that the Cordillera is a collage of terranes of different origin. (1982). The Telkwa Formation is part of the Hazelton Group and was selected for this study because it has been biochronologically dated, crops out over an extensive region of the central Stikine Terrane, and has bedding attitudes to define the palaeohorizontal unlike plutonic rocks (e.g. Beck Burmester & Schoonover 1981; Irving et al. 1985). Thus it is possible to relate the directions of remanent magnetizations to the estimated palaeohorizontal when the primary remanence is acquired. Previous palaeomagnetic work on the volcanic rocks of the Hazelton Group by Monger & Irving (1980) was restricted to areas near the eastern margin of Stikinia (Hl, H2, H3; Fig. 1). Their results suggested that Stikinia had been translated northward by -1300 km as well as rotated substantially about vertical axes. This interpretation was based on the best available reference pole at that time (Irving 1979). Although, the precision of their Hazelton Group result is somewhat low, the interpretation was supported by results from the Takla Group and Axelgold intrusion (Monger & Irving 1980). Key words: Cordilleran tectonics, Early Jurassic, Hazelton Group palaeomagnet- ism, Telkwa Formation, Terrane I. 1 INTRODUCTION The tectonic development of the Canadian Cordillera reflects the complex evolution of a collage of allochthonous terranes. Palaeomagnetism has been useful in studying this development by providing quantitative analyses of large- scale tectonic motions within and between terranes. The first aberrant palaeomagnetic result in the western Cordillera of North America came from the Eocene Siletz River Volcanic series of Oregon (Cox 1957). However, it was not until later that Irving (1964) recognized that this aberrant result was caused by rotation about a vertical axis. Since then numerous discordant palaeomagnetic results, together with differences between Cordilleran and contiguous North American stratigraphies and differences between coeval faunas along the ancient cratonic margin, have led to the recognition that the Cordillera is a collage of terranes of different origin. The samples were oriented by magnetic compass in the field and cored in the laboratory. Cores were sliced into one to three specimens (2.5cm diameter, and 2:5 cm height) and their natural remanent magnetization (NRM) was measured with a digital Schonstedt DSM-1 spinner magnetometer. Usually two specimens per sample were stepwise demagnetized in alternating fields (AF), in 12 steps up to 100 mT using a Schonstedt GSD-1 demagnetizer. The residual static field in the shield is less than 10nT. Unreliable measurements were repeated or discarded. Thermomagnetic curves were measured in air for 10 representative samples from the two occurrences using a recording Curie balance in an applied field of 3.1 A m-'. Initial susceptibility was measured by an inductometer. The mineralogy was investigated by reflected-light microscopy (one polished surface from each hand sample). Only 20 are from the mainly conglomeratic Dhan Khola Beds at the top of the section. In order to obtain a better resolution, 74 additional oriented clay samples were collected there. However, the clay samples yield no consistent behaviour. This paper is therefore concerned with sandstone samples only. Despite lithological differences (e.g. grain size and colour) of sandstones within the section, the demagnetization behaviour is quite homogeneous. For the thermal treatment shielded SCHONSTEDT or MMTDM furnaces were used. Susceptibility measurements after each step of heating enabled a control of possible mineral alterations. Received 1990 September 28; in original form 1990 July 2 SUMMARY Magnetostratigraphic age dating has been carried out on sandstones of a well- exposed continuous 5500 m thick Miocene-Pleistocene section in the Surai Khola area (West Nepal). The section is situated in the Siwalik Range which consists of molasse sediments from the Himalaya. Progressive demagnetization and isothermal remanence experiments prove that haematite is the carrier of the characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) throughout the entire section. The final polarity sequence is based on 436 samples, of which 233 have normal and 203 reverse polarity. Antiparallel mean directions of the normally and reversely polarized samples indicate that the ChRM is of primary origin. Comparison of the polarity sequence with a standard polarity time-scale yields a time period for the section between chron lr or chron 2r (Matuyama) and probably chron 5AB (between 1-2 Myr and about 13 Myr). e Siwalik Range is formed by Miocene to Pleistocene molasse sediments to the south of the Himalayas. Since 1983 lithological, biostratigraphic and archaeologi- cal studies have been in progress in the Surai Khola area of West Nepal (Fig. 1) (Corvinus 1988). This study is concerned with a continuous, well-exposed, sedimentary section of about 5500 m thickness. The section consists of 60°-800 northward dipping and WNW-ESE striking sediments without any major tectonic disturbances. It represents continuous fluvial sedimentation during the Neogene period. The section is composed of interbedded conglomerates (mainly in the upper part), sandstones, clays, shales and siltstones (Fig. 3). The grain size of the sandstones coarsens from the lower to the upper part of the section. A lithostratigraphic subdivision into six units (Bankas, Waterspring, Chor Khola, Surai Khola, Dobatta and Dhan Khola Beds) has been proposed by Corvinus (1988). Detailed biostratigraphic age dating seems to be impossible, and radiometrically datable volcanic ashes have not yet been detected. The volcanoes generally rise only a few hundred metres above the plateau surface and are steepsided with a central crater, which in some places measures more than half a kilometre in diameter. Some of the cones are built up of ash and scoriaceous lava while others are of more massive basalt. The thickness of the basalt flows is limited by the depth of the pre-existing valleys and rarely exceeds about 300 m in most cases, while the more extensive basalt sheets are made up of several flows. The large Kassa newer basalt (Fig. 1) includes several distinct petrographic types, and drilling to the west of Kassa has intercepted a horizon of sediments and decomposed rock between two distinct basalt flows. The basalts of the western plateau and the Panyam volcanic line have been described by Falconer (1926) and Mackay, Greenwood & Rockingham (1949). A group of large lateritized basalt remnants lie to the south of Jos on each side of the Bukuru road in the vicinity of the old airport. PALAEOMAGNETISM The direction and intensity of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) was measured using an astatic magnetometer. The required field free space was provided by a system of square Helmholtz coils. The mean direction of remanent magnetization and statistical parameters for each site were obtained using the method of Fisher (1953). Alternating field (AF) demagnetization was used to test the stability of NRM of each group of samples. The AF demagnetization was carried out using a rotatory tumbling device for simultaneously rotating the specimen about two mutually perpendicular axes while the demagnetizing alternating field was being applied. The remanent magnetism of the Vom Volcanics (latitude 9.7"N and longitude 8.9OE) were studied by Nwachuku (1977). He reported a stable site mean direction 'of declination = 354" and inclination = -6" from measurements on six cores drilled at this site, which has been dated as 0.9 f 0.2 Ma by the potassium-argon method (Grant, Rex & Freeth 1972). Since the volcanicity in this area spans a long interval of time during which the earth's main geomagnetic field has undergone several polarity reversals, Nwachuku (1977) suggested a 'piecemeal' approach with appropriate good age control for meaningful interpretation as a suitable approach to the palaeomagnetic study of these volcanics. The present study is spread over 10 different sites on and around the Jos Plateau between latitudes 9.0" and 10.O"N and longitudes 8.5" and 9.5"E. GEOLOGY The igneous rocks of post-Palaeozoic age in Nigeria can be divided into the following three main groups; the Jurassic Younger Granites and associated rocks, the Cretaceous intrusions and the products of Tertiary to Recent volcanic activities. Two different periods of volcanic activity

which affected parts of the Jos Plateau led to the formation of the volcanic rocks, often referred to as the Newer Basalts, in that area with an age range of 0.7-22 Ma (Macleod, Turner & Wright 1971). Grant et al. (1972), using the K-Ar method, dated rocks from Kass Hill as 1.5 f 0.1 Ma, Vom as 0.9 f 0.2 Ma and Bassa as 2.1 f 0.1 Ma. All these localities are from the rock unit A of this study which consists of sites 1 to 8. The ages of 1.5 and 2.1 for Kass Hill and Bassa respectively from the same group of rocks show that the volcanicity spanned a significant interval of time during which the earth's field may have undergone some polarity reversals. The samples from rock unit B (sites 9 and 10) show a reversed polarity. More K-Ar age determinations for rocks in this area are still to be carried out. REMANENCE AND TRM DEVIATION ANALYSIS The comparison of area mean directions (Fig. 6d; Tables 2 and 3) suggests that remanence acquisition post-dates local folding and/or rotational thrusting, and components B and C most likely relate to post-metamorphic cooling/uplift or phases of thermal overprinting. Thermo-remanent magnetization (TRM) acquisition in anisotropic rocks may involve considerable remanence deviation. Remanence deviation depends on grain-size, the degree of remanence anisotropy and more importantly on the angular relationship between the inducing ambient field and the pre-existing magnetic foliation.

Received 1990 May 15; in original form 1990 January 22 SUMMARY Based on new palaeomagnetic results from the North Norwegian Caledonides, we propose new apparent polar wander paths for Baltica during the Early-Mid Palaeozoic and discuss their palaeogeographic implications. In Cambrian and Early Ordovician times, Baltica occupied southerly latitudes of the order of 30" to SO", but was 'inverted' with respect to its present orientation. Consequently, the Russian Platform faced Avalonia and Gondwana, the latter continent occupying high southerly latitudes. Closure of the Tornquist Sea was then accompanied by continental scale, anticlockwise rotation of Baltica relative to Avalonia. This rotation probably occurred during mid-Ordovician times, although as yet, the timing of final suturing is poorly constrained

REGIONAL GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING Two major orogenic events have been postulated for the development of the northern Scandinavian Caledonides, i.e. a Late-Cambrian-Early-Ordovician event, known as the ‘Finnmarkian’ and a Silurian to Early Devonian, ‘Scandian’ event (Sturt, Miller & Fitch 1967; Pringle & Sturt 1969; Sturt, Pringle & Ramsay 1978; Ramsay et al. 1985; Roberts 1988a). Western Finnmark (Fig. 1) is characterized by a series of nappes and thrust sheets. The uppermost Mager~y Nappe was emplaced by Scandian thrusting, with the syn-orogenic but pre-thrusting Finnvik granite on Magereiy dated at 411 f 7 Ma (Rb/Sr whole rock; Andersen et al. 1982). The underlying Kalak Nappe Complex (KNC; Fig. 1) comprises a variety of rock units of different ages. A psammitic sequence (Klubben Group) predominates, passing up into pelites, limestones and finally turbidites (see reviews in Ramsay et al. 1985; Gayer et al. 1987). A Late Proterozoic to Cambrian age has been assumed for this succession, but some parts may be older than c. 800 Ma (Aitcheson, Daly & Cliff 1989). REMANENCE AND TRM DEVIATION ANALYSIS The comparison of area mean directions (Fig. 6d; Tables 2 and 3) suggests that remanence acquisition post-dates local folding and/or rotational thrusting, and components B and C most likely relate to post-metamorphic cooling/uplift or phases of thermal overprinting. Thermo-remanent magnetization (TRM) acquisition in anisotropic rocks may involve considerable remanence deviation. Remanence deviation depends on grain-size, the degree of remanence anisotropy and more importantly on the angular relationship between the inducing ambient field and the pre-existing magnetic foliation.

Trench' 'Department of Earth Sciences, The University, Oxford OX1 3PR, UK 2Norwegian Geological Survey, N-7002 Trondheim, Norway 'Department of Geology, University College, Galway, Ireland Accepted 1990 May 24. Received 1990 May 15; in original form 1990 January 22 SUMMARY Based on new palaeomagnetic results from the North Norwegian Caledonides, we propose new apparent polar wander paths for Baltica during the Early-Mid Palaeozoic and discuss their palaeogeographic implications. In Cambrian and Early Ordovician times, Baltica occupied southerly latitudes of the order of 30" to SO", but was 'inverted' with respect to its present orientation. Consequently, the Russian Platform faced Avalonia and Gondwana, the latter continent occupying high southerly latitudes. Closure of the Tornquist Sea was then accompanied by continental scale, anticlockwise rotation of Baltica relative to Avalonia. This rotation probably occurred during mid-Ordovician times, although as yet, the timing of final suturing is poorly constrained

Received 1990 May 15; in original form 1990 January 22 SUMMARY Based on new palaeomagnetic results from the North Norwegian Caledonides, we propose new apparent polar wander paths for Baltica during the Early-Mid Palaeozoic and discuss their palaeogeographic implications. In Cambrian and Early Ordovician times, Baltica occupied southerly latitudes of the order of 30" to SO", but was 'inverted' with respect to its present orientation. Consequently, the Russian Platform faced Avalonia and Gondwana, the latter continent occupying high southerly latitudes. Closure of the Tornquist Sea was then accompanied by continental scale, anticlockwise rotation of Baltica relative to Avalonia. This rotation probably occurred during mid-Ordovicia

Received 1990 May 15; in original form 1990 January 22 SUMMARY Based on new palaeomagnetic results from the North Norwegian Caledonides, we propose new apparent polar wander paths for Baltica during the Early-Mid Palaeozoic and discuss their palaeogeographic implications. In Cambrian and Early Ordovician times, Baltica occupied southerly latitudes of the order of 30" to SO", but was 'inverted' with respect to its present orientation. Consequently, the Russian Platform faced Avalonia and Gondwana, the latter continent occupying high southerly latitudes. Closure of the Tornquist Sea was then accompanied by continental scale, anticlockwise rotation of Baltica relative to Avalonia. This rotation probably occurred during mid-Ordovician times, although as yet, the timing of final suturing is poorly constrained

REGIONAL GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING Two major orogenic events have been postulated for the development of the northern Scandinavian Caledonides, i.e. a Late-Cambrian-Early-Ordovician event, known as the ‘Finnmarkian’ and a Silurian to Early Devonian, ‘Scandian’ event (Sturt, Miller & Fitch 1967; Pringle & Sturt 1969; Sturt, Pringle & Ramsay 1978; Ramsay et al. 1985; Roberts 1988a). Western Finnmark (Fig. 1) is characterized by a series of nappes and thrust sheets. The uppermost Mager~y Nappe was emplaced by Scandian thrusting, with the syn-orogenic but pre-thrusting Finnvik granite on Magereiy dated at 411 f 7 Ma (Rb/Sr whole rock; Andersen et al. 1982). The underlying Kalak Nappe Complex (KNC; Fig. 1) comprises a variety of rock units of different ages. A psammitic sequence (Klubben Group) predominates, passing up into pelites, limestones and finally turbidites (see reviews in Ramsay et al. 1985; Gayer et al. 1987). A Late Proterozoic to Cambrian age has been assumed for this succession, but some parts may be older than c. 800 Ma (Aitcheson, Daly & Cliff 1989). , Southern Britain. 1 INTRODUCTION The Ordovician palaeopositions of Laurentia and Gond- wana are now reasonably constrained to equatorial-trop- ical and high southerly latitudes respectively, based on palaeomagnetic data (reviews by Torsvik et al. 1990a; Bachtadse & Briden 1990). In addition, palaeomagnetic data from Baltica suggest it moved northward from c. 60"s to tropical southerly latitudes during Ordovician times (Torsvik et al. 1990b; Torsvik & Trench 1990). The latitudinal position of Southern Britain, however, is both enigmatic and contentious. This reflects a lack of palaeomagnetic studies which employ modern detailed demagnetization experiments in combination with appropri- ate field tests to constrain the relative age of magnetization. Middle Ordovician palaeomagnetic data from Southern Britain imply either mid-southerly palaeolatitudes (Briden, Turnell & Watts 1984; Briden et al. 1988) or somewhat higher southerly latitudes (Piper et al. 1978; Thomas & Briden 1976; McCabe & Channel1 1990a). , Southern Britain. 1 INTRODUCTION The Ordovician palaeopositions of Laurentia and Gond- wana are now reasonably constrained to equatorial-trop- ical and high southerly latitudes respectively, based on palaeomagnetic data (reviews by Torsvik et al. 1990a; Bachtadse & Briden 1990). In addition, palaeomagnetic data from Baltica suggest it moved northward from c. 60"s to tropical southerly latitudes during Ordovician times (Torsvik et al. 1990b; Torsvik & Trench 1990). The latitudinal position of Southern Britain, however, is both enigmatic and contentious. This reflects a lack of palaeomagnetic studies which employ modern detailed demagnetization experiments in combination with appropri- ate field tests to constrain the relative age of magnetization. Middle Ordovician palaeomagnetic data from Southern Britain imply either mid-southerly palaeolatitudes (Briden, Turnell & Watts 1984; Briden et al. 1988) or somewhat higher southerly latitudes (Piper et al. 1978; Thomas & Briden 1976; McCabe & Channel1 1990a). They also extend sporadically into the metamorphic terrane to the south (Stillman 1981) but are not found in Ordovician rocks overthrust from the north; magma ascent was concentrated along the tectonic boundary between these terranes (McKerrow & Campbell 1960). With the exception of sparse dolerite dykes which are largely unaltered and linked on structural, petrographic (Mohr 1982), radiometric (Mitchell & Mohr 1987) and palaeomagnetic (P. Dagley, personal communication) evidence to later events, these intrusions are altered with ubiquitous development of secondary chlorite, calcite and quartz. They were mostly emplaced prior to folding and faulting, and before full dewatering of the host sediments (McKerrow & Campbell 1960). According to McKerrow & Campbell they include dykes and sills of lamprophyre, microgranodiorite, andesite and felsite. Received 1991 January 16; in original form 1990 March 26 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetism of a Silurian succession (Lough Mask Formation lavas and sediments) and intrusive rocks (Kilbride dolerites and andesites and micrograno- diorites, Killary Harbour area) in the Connemara-Mayo segment of the Irish Caledonides is described. Magnetizations are related to the regional tectonic history with the aid of fold, conglomerate and contact tests. They describe sequences of shallow to intermediate inclinations in both the eastern and western sectors of this Caledonian inlier. The shallow components appear to pre-date Siluro-Devonian folding while the intermediate ones post-date this episode. The change in palaeofield inclination is identical to the transition described by contemporaneous deep level (Silurian) to shallow and surface level (Lower Devonian) bodies in the British and Scandinavian Caledonides but declinations are rotated consistently to the west. The Lower-Middle Silurian vector is rotated clockwise by c. 100". This difference is progressively reduced to c. 50" b

In addition igneous units are investigated comprising dykes and sills intruding the Silurian and Dalradian rocks spanning the exposed width of the inlier between Killary Bay in the west and the Kilbride Peninsula bordering Lough Mask in the east. These bodies range from mid-Silurian to mid-Carboniferous in age (Mitchell & Mohr 1987) and are cut by sparse younger dykes belonging to the Tertiary igneous province (Mohr 1982). The collective data are integrated here with the earlier palaeomagnetic results to clarify Siluro-Devonian apparent polar wander (APW) and derive a model of progressive deformation within this sector of the Caledonian orogenic belt. 2 GEOLOGICAL OUTLINE 2.1 Llandovery sediments and lavas Late Ordovician deformation in the South Mayo Trough (Phillips & Holland 1981) resulted in a major unconformity between Ordovician and Silurian successions. Magnetizations are related to the regional tectonic history with the aid of fold, conglomerate and contact tests. The shallow components appear to pre-date Siluro-Devonian folding while the intermediate ones post-date this episode. The change in palaeofield inclination is identical to the transition described by contemporaneous deep level (Silurian) to shallow and surface level (Lower Devonian) bodies in the British and Scandinavian Caledonides but declinations are rotated consistently to the west. Numerous studies of Tertiary to Recent orogenic zones have shown that palaeomagnetism can provide critical data for identifying allochthonous terranes and delimiting their kinematic history. Magnetic directions are of most value if field tests can establish their ages relative to tectonic events. Pre-emplacement remanences then constrain displacements with respect to the adjoining cratonic forelands, while the history of magnetic overprinting is of value as an indicator of (a) tectonic and/or thermal events related to terrane docking, (b) thermoviscous remanence (Kent & Miller 1985) or (c) thermochemical effects linked to fluid expulsion during orogenic loading (Oliver 1986). Few studies have used palaeomagnetism to unravel the tectonic history of pre-Tertiary terranes. However investi- gations to date suggest that the Caledonides of western Ireland are a promising area for application. Deutsch & Somayajulu (1970) first identified aberrant Ordovician declinations in the SMT. Received 1991 January 16; in original form 1990 March 26 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetism of a Silurian succession (Lough Mask Formation lavas and sediments) and intrusive rocks (Kilbride dolerites and andesites and micrograno- diorites, Killary Harbour area) in the Connemara-Mayo segment of the Irish Caledonides is described. Magnetizations are related to the regional tectonic history with the aid of fold, conglomerate and contact tests. They describe sequences of shallow to intermediate inclinations in both the eastern and western sectors of this Caledonian inlier. The shallow components appear to pre-date Siluro-Devonian folding while the intermediate ones post-date this episode. The change in palaeofield inclination is identical to the transition described by contemporaneous deep level (Silurian) to shallow and surface level (Lower Devonian) bodies in the British and Scandinavian Caledonides but declinations are rotated consistently to the west. The Lower-Middle Silurian vector is rotated clockwise by c. 100". This difference is progressively reduced to c. 50" b

In addition igneous units are investigated comprising dykes and sills intruding the Silurian and Dalradian rocks spanning the exposed width of the inlier between Killary Bay in the west and the Kilbride Peninsula bordering Lough Mask in the east. These bodies range from mid-Silurian to mid-Carboniferous in age (Mitchell & Mohr 1987) and are cut by sparse younger dykes belonging to the Tertiary igneous province (Mohr 1982). carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: he Main Donegal Granite shear zone where emplacement of the pluton at c. 400Ma occurred within the zone, and movements continued as the pluton consolidated (Halliday, Aftalion & Leake 1980; Hutton 1987). Numerous studies of Tertiary to Recent orogenic zones have shown that palaeomagnetism can provide critical data for identifying allochthonous terranes and delimiting their kinematic history. Magnetic directions are of most value if field tests can establish their ages relative to tectonic events. Pre-emplacement remanences then constrain displacements with respect to the adjoining cratonic forelands, while the history of magnetic overprinting is of value as an indicator of (a) tectonic and/or thermal events related to terrane docking, (b) thermoviscous remanence (Kent & Miller 1985) or (c) thermochemical effects linked to fluid expulsion during orogenic loading (Oliver 1986). Few studies have used palaeomagnetism to unravel the tectonic history of pre-Tertiary terranes. However investi- gations to date suggest that the Caledonides of western Ireland are a promising area for application. Deutsch & Somayajulu (1970) first identified aberrant Ordovician declinations in the SMT. Piper Geomagnetism Laboratory, Department of Earth Sciences, University of Liverpool, PO Box 147, Liverpool L69 3BX, UK Accepted 1991 March 18. Received 1991 January 16; in original form 1990 March 26 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetism of a Silurian succession (Lough Mask Formation lavas and sediments) and intrusive rocks (Kilbride dolerites and andesites and micrograno- diorites, Killary Harbour area) in the Connemara-Mayo segment of the Irish Caledonides is described. Magnetizations are related to the regional tectonic history with the aid of fold, conglomerate and contact tests. They describe sequences of shallow to intermediate inclinations in both the eastern and western sectors of this Caledonian inlier. The shallow components appear to pre-date Siluro-Devonian folding while the intermediate ones post-date this episode. The change in palaeofield inclination is identical to the transition described by contemporaneous deep level (Silurian) to shallow and surface level (Lower Devonian) bodies in the British and Scandinavian Caledonides but declinations are rotated consistently to the west. The Lower-Middle Silurian vector is rotated clockwise by c. 100". This difference is progressively reduced to c. 50" b

In addition igneous units are investigated comprising dykes and sills intruding the Silurian and Dalradian rocks spanning the exposed width of the inlier between Killary Bay in the west and the Kilbride Peninsula bordering Lough Mask in the east. These bodies range from mid-Silurian to mid-Carboniferous in age (Mitchell & Mohr 1987) and are cut by sparse younger dykes belonging to the Tertiary igneous province (Mohr 1982). The collective data are integrated here with the earlier palaeomagnetic results to clarify Siluro-Devonian apparent polar wander (APW) and derive a model of progressive deformation within this sector of the Caledonian orogenic belt. 2 GEOLOGICAL OUTLINE 2.1 Llandovery sediments and lavas Late Ordovician deformation in the South Mayo Trough (Phillips & Holland 1981) resulted in a major unconformity between Ordovician and Silurian successions. They also extend sporadically into the metamorphic terrane to the south (Stillman 1981) but are not found in Ordovician rocks overthrust from the north; magma ascent was concentrated along the tectonic boundary between these terranes (McKerrow & Campbell 1960). With the exception of sparse dolerite dykes which are largely unaltered and linked on structural, petrographic (Mohr 1982), radiometric (Mitchell & Mohr 1987) and palaeomagnetic (P. Dagley, personal communication) evidence to later events, these intrusions are altered with ubiquitous development of secondary chlorite, calcite and quartz. They were mostly emplaced prior to folding and faulting, and before full dewatering of the host sediments (McKerrow & Campbell 1960). According to McKerrow & Campbell they include dykes and sills of lamprophyre, microgranodiorite, andesite and felsite. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: he Main Donegal Granite shear zone where emplacement of the pluton at c. 400Ma occurred within the zone, and movements continued as the pluton consolidated (Halliday, Aftalion & Leake 1980; Hutton 1987). Numerous studies of Tertiary to Recent orogenic zones have shown that palaeomagnetism can provide critical data for identifying allochthonous terranes and delimiting their kinematic history. Magnetic directions are of most value if field tests can establish their ages relative to tectonic events. Pre-emplacement remanences then constrain displacements with respect to the adjoining cratonic forelands, while the history of magnetic overprinting is of value as an indicator of (a) tectonic and/or thermal events related to terrane docking, (b) thermoviscous remanence (Kent & Miller 1985) or (c) thermochemical effects linked to fluid expulsion during orogenic loading (Oliver 1986). Few studies have used palaeomagnetism to unravel the tectonic history of pre-Tertiary terranes. However investi- gations to date suggest that the Caledonides of western Ireland are a promising area for application. Deutsch & Somayajulu (1970) first identified aberrant Ordovician declinations in the SMT. Magnetizations are related to the regional tectonic history with the aid of fold, conglomerate and contact tests. They describe sequences of shallow to intermediate inclinations in both the eastern and western sectors of this Caledonian inlier. The shallow components appear to pre-date Siluro-Devonian folding while the intermediate ones post-date this episode. The change in palaeofield inclination is identical to the transition described by contemporaneous deep level (Silurian) to shallow and surface level (Lower Devonian) bodies in the British and Scandinavian Caledonides but declinations are rotated consistently to the west. However investi- gations to date suggest that the Caledonides of western Ireland are a promising area for application. The results are only in part compatible with data from the strike continuation of the Caledonides in Britain, and a range of tectonic interpretations have been proposed. Few studies have used palaeomagnetism to unravel the tectonic history of pre-Tertiary terranes. However investi- gations to date suggest that the Caledonides of western Ireland are a promising area for application. Deutsch & Somayajulu (1970) first identified aberrant Ordovician declinations in the SMT. Subsequent studies resolved a remanence record within the DMT (Morris et al. 1973; Morris & Tanner 1977; Robertson 1988) and the SMT (Morris et al. 1973; Morris 1976; Deutsch & Storetvedt 1988; Smethurst & Briden 1988). The results are only in part compatible with data from the strike continuation of the Caledonides in Britain, and a range of tectonic interpretations have been proposed. The present study covers the lower part of the Silurian succession lying unconformably on Dalradian rocks near the eastern margin of the outcrop. They also extend sporadically into the metamorphic terrane to the south (Stillman 1981) but are not found in Ordovician rocks overthrust from the north; magma ascent was concentrated along the tectonic boundary between these terranes (McKerrow & Campbell 1960). With the exception of sparse dolerite dykes which are largely unaltered and linked on structural, petrographic (Mohr 1982), radiometric (Mitchell & Mohr 1987) and palaeomagnetic (P. Dagley, personal communication) evidence to later events, these intrusions are altered with ubiquitous development of secondary chlorite, calcite and quartz. They were mostly emplaced prior to folding and faulting, and before full dewatering of the host sediments (McKerrow & Campbell 1960). Magnetizations are related to the regional tectonic history with the aid of fold, conglomerate and contact tests. They describe sequences of shallow to intermediate inclinations in both the eastern and western sectors of this Caledonian inlier. The shallow components appear to pre-date Siluro-Devonian folding while the intermediate ones post-date this episode. The change in palaeofield inclination is identical to the transition described by cont

g cratonic forelands, while the history of magnetic overprinting is of value as an indicator of (a) tectonic and/or thermal events related to terrane docking, (b) thermoviscous remanence (Kent & Miller 1985) or (c) thermochemical effects linked to fluid expulsion during orogenic loading (Oliver 1986). Few studies have used palaeomagnetism to unravel the tectonic history of pre-Tertiary terranes. However investi- gations to date suggest that the Caledonides of western Ireland are a promising area for application. Deutsch & Somayajulu (1970) first identified aberrant Ordovician declinations in the SMT. Subsequent studies resolved a remanence record within the DMT (Morris et al. 1973; Morris & Tanner 1977; Robertson 1988) and the SMT (Morris et al. 1973; Morris 1976; Deutsch & Storetvedt 1988; Smethurst & Briden 1988). The results are only in part compatible with data from the strike continuation of the Caledonides in Britain, and a range of tectonic interpretations have been proposed. The present study covers the lower part of the Silurian succession lying unconformably on Dalradian rocks near the eastern margin of the outcrop. In particular, reliable data, substantiated by a magnetic-polarity stratigraphy, have been obtained from undeformed Ordovician carbonates of the Swedish platform (Torsvik & Trench 1990, 1991; Perroud, Robardet & Bruton 1991). The APWP implies that Baltica occupied temperate southerly latitudes in the Late Cambrian and then moved northward during the Ordovician whilst undergoing counter-clockwise rotation. This problem led Torsvik et af. (1990a) to propose two alternative Silurian path segments for Baltica which they termed path-options X and Y (Fig. 1). The present study was therefore initiated in an attempt to discriminate between paths X and Y and to time-calibrate Silurian APW relative to Baltica. In the latter respect, the rich fauna of the Gotland limestones provides an excellent stratigraphic constraint if one considers that the rock age and magnetization age coincide. Received 1991 June 13; in original form 1991 February 6 SUMMARY Well-dated and undeformed Silurian (Lower Wenlock) limestones from Gotland, southern Sweden, yield two stable remanence components following detailed thermal and alternating-field demagnetization studies. (1) A low blocking-temperature/coercivity magnetization, termed L, delineated below 250 "C/lO mT, is oriented parallel to the present Earth's field (Dec. 001, Inc. +67, n = 4 sites, uq5 = 16"). (2) A higher blocking-temperature/coercivity magnetization, termed H, un- blocked between 250-400 "C/10-35 mT, has a NNE declination and shallow negative inclination (Dec. 025, Inc. -19, n = 5 sites, uqs =So). This H component direction compares favourably with a previous result from Gotland based upon blanket cleaning. Given a lack of evidence for subsequent geological heating (Conodont Alteration Index = 1-lS), or pervasive palaeomagnetic overprinting, the H palaeopole is regarded as reliable and primary/early diagenetic in origin (19"S, 352"E, dpldm 3/5). This H component direction compares favourably with a previous result from Gotland based upon blanket cleaning. Given a lack of evidence for subsequent geological heating (Conodont Alteration Index = 1-lS), or pervasive palaeomagnetic overprinting, the H palaeopole is regarded as reliable and primary/early diagenetic in origin (19"S, 352"E, dpldm 3/5). The only other well-constrained Mid-Silurian pole from Baltica, that from the Ringerike Sandstone of the Oslo district, is in excellent agreement with the Gotland data. These combined poles resolve previous problems regarding the shape and time-calibration of Silurian apparent polar wander relative to Baltica. Key words: Baltica, palaeomagnetism, Silurian, Sweden. INTRODUCTION Recently reported palaeomagnetic studies from Baltica have placed new constraints on its Lower Palaeozoic movement history. In particular, reliable data, substantiated by a magnetic-polarity stratigraphy, have been obtained from undeformed Ordovician carbonates of the Swedish platform (Torsvik & Trench 1990, 1991; Perroud, Robardet & Bruton 1991). This problem led Torsvik et af. (1990a) to propose two alternative Silurian path segments for Baltica which they termed path-options X and Y (Fig. 1). The present study was therefore initiated in an attempt to discriminate between paths X and Y and to time-calibrate Silurian APW relative to Baltica. In the latter respect, the rich fauna of the Gotland limestones provides an excellent stratigraphic constraint if one considers that the rock age and magnetization age coincide. PREVIOUS PALAEOMAGNETIC WORK A previous palaeomagnetic investigation of the Gotland limestones was undertaken by Claesson (1979) using a Digico spinner magnetometer to measure the natural remanent magnetization (NRM). In an extensive sampling (84 sites), only a subordinate number of specimens were found to retain a repeatabfy measurable NRM after blanket demagnetization at 150 "C (occasionally 250 "C). carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: The present study was therefore initiated in an attempt to remedy this point and describes a palaeomagnetic survey of the Early Ordovician Treffgarne Volcanic Formation, SW Dyfed, Wales. 2 GEOLOGICAL BACKGROUND AND PALAEOMAGNETIC SAMPLING The Treffgarne Volcanic Formation (TVF) is of late Tremadoc to early Arenig age (Traynor 1988; Fortey & Owens 1987, 1990) and forms the local base of the Gwynedd Supergroup in the southern Welsh Basin (Woodcock 1990). The volcanics are most likely of volcanic arc affinity and have been tentatively correlated (Traynor 1988) with the Rhobell Volcanic Complex in the central part of the basin (Kokelaar 1979; Kokelaar et al. 1984). The type section of the TVF is exposed at Treffgarne Gorge, approximately 8 km North of Haverfordwest, Dyfed (Fig, 1). The TVF comprises andesitic lavas, which are overlain by volcaniclastic and epiclastic sediments. A total of 15 palaeomagnetic sites were sampled within quarries along the A40 (Fig. 1). Sites 1-3 comprise coarse-grained sandstones and purple laminated mudstones. Sites 4-7 are from bedded volcaniclastic deposits. Site 7 embraces a boulder conglomerate containing clasts of the underlying andesites (Thomas & Cox 1924). Sites 8-15 represent andesite lavas. The volcanics and sediments dip

etic sampling sites. Inset: relative Ordovician stratigraphy of volcanic inliers. Arenig stages from Fortey & Owens (1987). average dip from the overlying beds. Northward tilting of the TVF occurred either during Acadian (Woodcock et al. 1988) or Hercynian deformation (Hancock, Dunne & Tringham 1981). Metamorphism is low-grade (anchizone) with palaeotemperatures in the order of 200"-300 "C (summarized by Oliver 1988). 3 FIELD AND LABORATORY METHODS Individual core samples were oriented using a magnetic compass. Bearings were later corrected for a local deviation of 7" west at the sampling site. Samples were treated using stepwise thermal demagnetization. The alternating-field method had earlier failed to achieve a satisfactory cleaning of directions (Almond 1971; described in Morris et al. 1973). The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of samples was measured with a two-axis CCL superconducting magneto- meter. Component analysis of demagnetization data was performed using least-squares line-fitting algorithms (Kent, Briden & Mardia 1983; Torsvik 1986), aided by inspection of orthogonal and stereographic projections. 4 ROCK MAGNETIC PROPERTIES Thermomagnetic analyses Thermomagnetic analyses reveal both magnetite/low- titanium titanomagnetite and haematite magnetic phases within

In Figs 2(b) and (d), magnetite (580°C) and haematite (670OC) Curie points are identified during heating and cooling cycles. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: The present study was therefore initiated in an attempt to remedy this point and describes a palaeomagnetic survey of the Early Ordovician Treffgarne Volcanic Formation, SW Dyfed, Wales. 2 GEOLOGICAL BACKGROUND AND PALAEOMAGNETIC SAMPLING The Treffgarne Volcanic Formation (TVF) is of late Tremadoc to early Arenig age (Traynor 1988; Fortey & Owens 1987, 1990) and forms the local base of the Gwynedd Supergroup in the southern Welsh Basin (Woodcock 1990). The volcanics are most likely of volcanic arc affinity and have been tentatively correlated (Traynor 1988) with the Rhobell Volcanic Complex in the central part of the basin (Kokelaar 1979; Kokelaar et al. 1984). The type section of the TVF is exposed at Treffgarne Gorge, approximately 8 km North of Haverfordwest, Dyfed (Fig, 1). The TVF comprises andesitic lavas, which are overlain by volcaniclastic and epiclastic sediments. A total of 15 palaeomagnetic sites were sampled within quarries along the A40 (Fig. 1). Sites 1-3 comprise coarse-grained sandstones and purple laminated mudstones. Sites 4-7 are from bedded volcaniclastic deposits. Site 7 embraces a boulder conglomerate containing clasts of the underlying andesites (Thomas & Cox 1924). Sites 8-15 represent andesite lavas. The volcanics and sediments dip

etic sampling sites. Inset: relative Ordovician stratigraphy of volcanic inliers. Arenig stages from Fortey & Owens (1987). average dip from the overlying beds. Northward tilting of the TVF occurred either during Acadian (Woodcock et al. 1988) or Hercynian deformation (Hancock, Dunne & Tringham 1981). Metamorphism is low-grade (anchizone) with palaeotemperatures in the order of 200"-300 "C (summarized by Oliver 1988). 3 FIELD AND LABORATORY METHODS Individual core samples were oriented using a magnetic compass. Bearings were later corrected for a local deviation of 7" west at the sampling site. Samples were treated using stepwise thermal demagnetization. The alternating-field method had earlier failed to achieve a satisfactory cleaning of directions (Almond 1971; described in Morris et al. 1973). The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of samples was measured with a two-axis CCL superconducting magneto- meter. Component analysis of demagnetization data was performed using least-squares line-fitting algorithms (Kent, Briden & Mardia 1983; Torsvik 1986), aided by inspection of orthogonal and stereographic projections. 4 ROCK MAGNETIC PROPERTIES Thermomagnetic analyses Thermomagnetic analyses reveal both magnetite/low- titanium titanomagnetite and haematite magnetic phases within

This pole, located at N56", E306" (dpldm = 9/10), implies that Southern Britain was positioned at c. 60"s during Early Ordovician times. These data are considered palaeomagnetically reliable based upon a positive intraformational conglomerate test. Geological indicators of palaeotemperature in the south/central Welsh Basin most likely reflect a Hercynian thermochemical pulse. The Middle Ordovician data set across Britain now implies that the Iapetus Ocean had a latitudinal width of c. 30" at this time. The latter estimate concurs with faunal interpretations of oceanic separation (Cocks & Fortey 1982, 1990). However, no reliable palaeomagnetic results exist for Early Ordovician times, the time of maximum faunal diversity (McKerrow & Cocks 1976, 1986). SAMPLING AND RESULTS The biotite granite of E1 Tiro was sampled at four unmin- eralized and relatively unaltered sites to the south and west of the E1 Tiro pit (Figure 2). The coarse-grained granite was sampled at three sites, and an aplite phase was sampled at site BG2. Oriented samples from 34 sites in volcanic, volcaniclastic, and intrusive units related to this episode of igneous activity (73-69 Ma) yield a mean paleomagnetic direction of I = 61.2 ø, D = 24.0 ø, a95 -- 7.6 ø. Primary remanent magnetizations are indicated by the presence of both normal and reversed polarities and by the significantly improved grouping (95% confidence level) of site-mean directions for a widespread tuff unit after structural correction. A comparison of this direction with a direction at Silver Bell calculated from contemporaneous units for stable North America (I = 58.8 ø, D = 342.3 ø, a95 -- 7.7 ø) indicates a Late Cretaceous paleolatitude anomaly of-2.4 ø +- 7.6 ø (not significant at the 95% confidence level) and a declination anomaly of 41.7 ø _ 14.3 ø for the Silver Bell Mountains. Previously determined paleomagnetic data for southeastern Arizona suggest that this apparent clockwise rotation in the Silver Bell Mountains is a local phenomenon. Although preliminary, the average paleomagnetic dir

s in the Silver Bell area (I -- 43.8 ø, D = 357.3 ø, a95 -- 16.5 ø) is similar to that calculated for stable North America (I = 50.2 ø, D - 352.2 ø, a95 = 3.9ø), implying that the observed rotation in the Silver Bell Mountains occurred before 26 Ma and was most likely associated with dextral strike-slip movement along the Ragged Top and related WNW trending faults bounding the Silver Bell Mountain block. These data, in conjunction with plate reconstructions and other paleomagnetic data from southwestern North America, imply that WNW trending strike-slip faults may have played an important role during Late Cretaceous to early Tertiary deformation in southerp Arizona. oth, relative to the North American continent [Beck, 1980]. Many of these displacements are probably caused by large-scale deformation associated with dextral shear between the North American plate and oceanic plates to the west since at least Late Cretaceous time [Beck, 1986]. SAWYER U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, Colorado Late Cretaceous ash flow volcanism in the Silver Bell Mountains of southern Arizona (32.3øN, 248.5øE) was associated with caldera formation and porphyry copper mineralization. Oriented samples from 34 sites in volcanic, volcaniclastic, and intrusive units related to this episode of igneous activity (73-69 Ma) yield a mean paleomagnetic direction of I = 61.2 ø, D = 24.0 ø, a95 -- 7.6 ø. Primary remanent magnetizations are indicated by the presence of both normal and reversed polarities and by the significantly improved grouping (95% confidence level) of site-mean directions for a widespread tuff unit after structural correction. A comparison of this direction with a direction at Silver Bell calculated from contemporaneous units for stable North America (I = 58.8 ø, D = 342.3 ø, a95 -- 7.7 ø) indicates a Late Cretaceous paleolatitude anomaly of-2.4 ø +- 7.6 ø (not significant at the 95% confidence level) and a declination anomaly of 41.7 ø _ 14.3 ø for the Silver Bell Mountains. Previously determined paleomagnetic data for southeastern Arizona suggest that this apparent clockwise rotation in the Silver Bell Mountains is a local phenomenon. Although preliminary, the average paleomagnetic dir

s in the Silver Bell area (I -- 43.8 ø, D = 357.3 ø, a95 -- 16.5 ø) is similar to that calculated for stable North America (I = 50.2 ø, D - 352.2 ø, a95 = 3.9ø), implying that the observed rotation in the Silver Bell Mountains occurred before 26 Ma and was most likely associated with dextral strike-slip movement along the Ragged Top and related WNW trending faults bounding the Silver Bell Mountain block. These data, in conjunction with plate reconstructions and other paleomagnetic data from southwestern North America, imply that WNW trending strike-slip faults may have played an important role during Late Cretaceous to early Tertiary deformation in southerp Arizona. INTRODUCTION Few paleomagnetic data for rocks of Late Cretaceous to early Tertiary (Laramide) age are available from the south- ern Basin and Range province of western North America (Figure 1). Paleomagnetic data determined for the Upper Cretaceous Roskruge Volcanics and the lower Paleocene Gringo Gulch Volcanics of southern Arizona [Vugteveen et al., 1981] are basically consistent with the North American apparent polar wander (APW) path but are limited and may not be representative of the entire region. More extensive paleomagnetic studies have been undertaken in Jurassic volcanic rocks from southeastern Ar

ary, and younger phases of Basin and Range extension along steeply dipping normal faults. Geological and geophysical investigations imply that much of the North American Cordillera is composed of tectono- stratigraphic terranes which are allochthonous with respect to the stable craton [Coney et al., 1980]. Paleomagnetic results for many of these terranes are consistently discordant with the North American APW path, indicating that they have undergone either northward translations or clockwise rotations, or both, relative to the North American continent [Beck, 1980]. Many of these displacements are probably caused by large-scale deformation associated with dextral shear between the North American plate and oceanic plates to the west since at least Late Cretaceous time [Beck, 1986]. In the Pacific Northwest a monotonic westward increase in the amount of rotation of crustal fragments argues in favor of distributed dextral shear as the cause of the rotations [e.g., Wells and Heller, 1988]. The proximity of southern Arizona to the western margin of North America implies that this region may also have been subjected to a similar style of deformation. Treatment Samples were measured and demagnetized within a steel magnetically shielded room. A computer- interfaced SCT cryogenic magnetometer, with a practical noise limit of 5 x 5 -6 A/m (5 x 10 -9 emu/cm3), was used for all measurements. Multiple readings per measurement were taken, according to the strength of the samples. Samples were demag- netized both in alternating fields AF (using a single axis Schonsted GSD-1 AF demagnetizer) and thermally. Thermal demagnetization employed a 25- sample horizontal oven, having an ambient field in the cooling chamber of 55 nT. Duplicate specimens of representative samples from each lithology at all localities were treated by both thermal and AF demagnetization. These pilot samples were stepwise AF demagnetized in fields of 5 to 40 mT. AF treatment produced sub- stantial intensity loss but no significant separa- tion of components by 40 mT; therefore demagne- tization was not continued in higher fields. Treatment Samples were measured and demagnetized within a steel magnetically shielded room. A computer- interfaced SCT cryogenic magnetometer, with a practical noise limit of 5 x 5 -6 A/m (5 x 10 -9 emu/cm3), was used for all measurements. Multiple readings per measurement were taken, according to the strength of the samples. Samples were demag- netized both in alternating fields AF (using a single axis Schonsted GSD-1 AF demagnetizer) and thermally. Thermal demagnetization employed a 25- sample horizontal oven, having an ambient field in the cooling chamber of 55 nT. Duplicate specimens of representative samples from each lithology at all localities were treated by both thermal and AF demagnetization. These pilot samples were stepwise AF demagnetized in fields of 5 to 40 mT. AF treatment produced sub- stantial intensity loss but no significant separa- tion of components by 40 mT; therefore demagne- tization was not continued in higher fields. Treatment Samples were measured and demagnetized within a steel magnetically shielded room. A computer- interfaced SCT cryogenic magnetometer, with a practical noise limit of 5 x 5 -6 A/m (5 x 10 -9 emu/cm3), was used for all measurements. Samples were demag- netized both in alternating fields AF (using a single axis Schonsted GSD-1 AF demagnetizer) and thermally. Thermal demagnetization employed a 25- sample horizontal oven, having an ambient field in the cooling chamber of 55 nT. Duplicate specimens of representative samples from each lithology at all localities were treated by both thermal and AF demagnetization. These pilot samples were stepwise AF demagnetized in fields of 5 to 40 mT. AF treatment produced sub- stantial intensity loss but no significant separa- tion of components by 40 mT; therefore demagne- tization was not continued in higher fields. Treatment Samples were measured and demagnetized within a steel magnetically shielded room. A computer- interfaced SCT cryogenic magnetometer, with a practical noise limit of 5 x 5 -6 A/m (5 x 10 -9 emu/cm3), was used for all measurements. Multiple readings per measurement were taken, according to the strength of the samples. Samples were demag- netized both in alternating fields AF (using a single axis Schonsted GSD-1 AF demagnetizer) and thermally. Thermal demagnetization employed a 25- sample horizontal oven, having an ambient field in the cooling chamber of 55 nT. Duplicate specimens of representative samples from each lithology at all localities were treated by both thermal and AF demagnetization. These pilot samples were stepwise AF demagnetized in fields of 5 to 40 mT. AF treatment produced sub- stantial intensity loss but no significant separa- tion of components by 40 mT; therefore demagne- tization was not continued in higher fields. We obtained two new K-At dates from the Adel rocks. One date, on biotite ( from a shonkinite dike that crosscuts most of the volcanic rocks, is 71.2 + 2.7 Ms. The other, a whole rock date from a flow deep in the volcanic pile, is 81.1 +_ 3.5 Ms. We collected six to nine palcomagnetic samples from each of 34 sites in roadcuts and natural outcrops of flows, dikes, and laccoliths. They reveal the evolution of the \"Armorican\" terranes [Van der Voo, 1979] initially situated at the margin of the West African craton, and then accreted to Eurasia. However, major questions remain unanswered: What was the timing of the docking? Was \"Armorica\" a separate plate, and if so what was its extent? According to their different magnetic properties, the results of the demagnetization procedures for the flows and the breccia will be discussed separately. Demagnetization Results From the Tuffs Three components of magnetization were revealed at the eight breccia sites (Figure 6), upon thermal or af treatments. The first removed was found in all sites and disappears usually by 150ø-200øC or 20 mT. The direction for this component in field coordinates is similar to the present-day EMF direction, and it is dominant in some sites (compare sample AB 12, Figure 6) with a high-alteration state. It was therefore interpreted as a recent overprint due to in situ alteration processes. Above 200øC, most sites display a shallow-eastward component, which can dominate the rest of the NRM (sample AE29, Figure 6), but in all cases the demagnetization trajectories do not converge toward the origin. By 450øC or 50 mT, final northeast and slightly upward directions are reached for some samples from sites AD, AJ and AK (Figure 6). For site AI, similar endpoints were observed, but with shallow-westward directions. However, there are indications for another magnetic phase that loses its magnetization between 300 ø and 350øC, as revealed by sample AM91, or by the difference between the heating and cooling curves for AR14. This second phase (maghemite?) is probably carrying the NRM of site AM samples since they have very similar unblocking temperatures (Figure 8). The comparison of AMS and paleomagnetic results reveal clear relationships between them. In site AY, for example, the high-temperature components were obtained mainly in the high-susceptibility samples (compare AY63, Figure 8), while separation of components was not successful in the low-susceptibility samples (compare AY66, Figure 9). Intensity of magnetization is also very much higher in the former. It seems therefore that the large primary magnetite grains observed in the high-susceptibility samples, which present reversible thermomagnetic behavior and Curie points at 580øC, are actually carrying the high-temperature component. As they have recorded emplacement features in the AMS, we believe that they have originated very early in the crystallization process, and they can therefore carry the primary magnetization of the Almaden lavas. They reveal the evolution of the \"Armorican\" terranes [Van der Voo, 1979] initially situated at the margin of the West African craton, and then accreted to Eurasia. However, major questions remain unanswered: What was the timing of the docking? Was \"Armorica\" a separate plate, and if so what was its extent? New data from intermediate periods are necessary to resolve such questions. In this paper we report new paleomagnetic results from the Silurian volcanism of the Almaden mining district, situated in southern Spain. As no fully reliable data are available for the Silurian period from southern Europe, it was extremely important to conduct a very detailed paleomagnetic analysis of this volcanic sequence. Preliminary results, from two sites, were reported in 1967 by Van der Voo [1967] showing a complex magnetization but also evidence for pretectonic components. EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES For our paleomagnetic study, we collected Mesozoic strata at 18 sites for a total of 306 samples (see Figure 1 for location of sampling areas). Half of the samples were measured at the Universidad Sim6n Bolivar using a Molspin magnetometer and a Schonstedt thermal or alternating field demagnetizer located inside three sets of Helmholtz coils. At the University of Texas, an ScT cryogenic magnetometer and Schonstedt furnace or AF unit were used, all of which are housed inside a magnetically shielded room. All samples were stepwise demagnetized, and the data were analyzed by the principal component method. Samples were excluded from the analysis of the site mean if either no stable component of magnetization could be identified or if their direction differed from the site mean by more than two angular standard deviations. MAGNETIC MINERALOGY The magnetic mineralogy of a limited number of samples was determined by analyzing their coercivity spectra and by microscopic examination of thin sections. GEISSMAN Department of Geology, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque Paleomagnetic data obtained from Oligocene to lower Miocene igneous rocks and middle Miocene basaltic rocks at fifteen localities from a region surrounding Dixie Valley in west central Nevada indicate that parts of the area experienced counterclockwise vertical-axis rotation, and these data provide constraints on the extent and timing of rotation. Counterclockwise vertical-axis rotation probably exceeding 30 ø is indicated for Oligocene to lower Miocene rocks in the central part of the study area. Calculated rotations increase with increasing age of the Oligocene to lower Miocene rocks, indicating that vertical-axis rotation was concuiTent with ash-flow deposition (about 23-33 Ma). Paleomagnetic data indicate that middle Miocene basa

saltic rocks at fifteen localities from a region surrounding Dixie Valley in west central Nevada indicate that parts of the area experienced counterclockwise vertical-axis rotation, and these data provide constraints on the extent and timing of rotation. Counterclockwise vertical-axis rotation probably exceeding 30 ø is indicated for Oligocene to lower Miocene rocks in the central part of the study area. Calculated rotations increase with increasing age of the Oligocene to lower Miocene rocks, indicating that vertical-axis rotation was concuiTent with ash-flow deposition (about 23-33 Ma). Paleomagnetic data indicate that middle Miocene basaltic rocks (about 10-17 Ma) postdate significant counterclockwise vertical-axis rotation, although this interpretation is complicated because the rocks were erupted episodically in pulses that apparently were short lived with respect to geomagnetic secular variation. Counterclockwise rotation was related to a deformation event that predated development of the present basin and range physiography of the area. The total amount of crustal rotation in Tertiary time in the area is poorly known.
