Rotation estimates calculated from time-averaged mean directions that incorporate data from a broad range of the Oligocene to lower Miocene units probably underestimate total Tertiary rotation because the mean directions include data from units that postdate much of the rotation. For example, a rotation estimate for a composite sequence from the central part of the study area is -23 ø _+ 15 ø, whereas estimates from older and younger halves of the sequence are -37 ø

At individual sites typically six to ten samples were collected from a single geologic unit over an area of several tens of square meters. All samples were collected with a portable drill and oriented using both magnetic and sun compasses. Attitudes of the strata used for tilt-correction of the paleomagnetic data were estimated from compaction foliations or boundaries of welding zones in tuffs, boundaries of flows in lavas, or bedding of sedimentary strata intercalated with the volcanic units. In the laboratory, remanent magnetizations were mea- sured with a Schonstedt DSM-1 spinner magnetometer. Alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetization of spec- imens were performed using Schonstedt GSD-5 and TSD-1 instruments, respectively. For most sites, detailed pilot demagnetization (10-15 steps) on one or two specimens was followed by demagnetization of the remaining samples, using 6-9 steps. AF demagnetization principally was used because it was effective in isolating a well-defined and well-grouped magnetization in most volcanic rocks. Representative sam- ples from many sites were thermally demagnetized for comparison with AF results and to assess unblocking tem- perature spectra of the units. In this paper we present the results from 373 oriented cores taken from one section representing 3 km of sedimentary rocks. The section is dated with continental ostracods and with a magnetostratigraphic correlation between a densely sampled 272-m sequence and the polarity time scale, giving an upper Jurassic to Upper Cretaceous or Lower Tertiary age. The remanent direction is remarkably stable throughout the section (D=2.0 ø, I=34.2 ø, k=63.1,ot9s=3.6 ø, N=26/28 sites). While this fact might suggest that the section has been remagnetized, paleomagnetic and rock magnetic tests indicate that the remanence is primary. The pole position (78.6øN, 273.4øE, dp=2.4 ø, din=4.1 ø) corresponds to a rather low paleolatitude (L*-18.8ø+2.4 ø) but is consistent with other Cretaceous poles from China. If one accepts the Eurasian APWP of Irving and Irving (1982), this result would imply that more than 1000 km of shortening took place between South China and Eurasia, following the acquisition of the remanence. However, there is no geological evidence for this large shortening. Paleomagnetism offers an independent possibility to constrain the geological history of Southeast Asia. Whereas geological evidence usually comes from the borders of the cratons, paleomag- netic investigations tend to focus on the stable interiors. Clearly, geodynamic interpretation of paleomagnetic data demands very well-determined apparent polar wander paths (APWPs). Besse [1986] and Besse and Courtillot [this issue] have reconsidered the corpus of published paleomagnetic data to propose reliable reference APWPs covering the last 200 Ma for some of the major continental blocks. Eighteen site-mean VGPs from the Owl Rock Member of the Chide Formation yield a middle Norian palw- magnetic pole position of 56.5'N. 66.4'E (K = 183, Ags = 2.6'). Twenty-three site-mean VGPs from the Kayenta Formation yield a Pliensbachian pole position of 59.0Â°N 66.6'E (K = 155, A95 = 2.4'). Combined with paleomagnetic poles from the Moenave Formation and the Shinarump Member of the Chinle Formation, these data record -30 m.y. of North American apparent polar wander (APW) within a regional stratigraphic succession. During the Camian and Norian stages of the Late Triassic, Chinle poles progress westward. During the Hettangian through Pliensbachian stages of the Early Jurassic, the pattern of APW changed to an eastward progression. Even after correction for 4' clockwise rota- tion of the Colorado Plateau, a sharp comer in the APW path (Jl cusp) is resolved near the pole from the HettangianLSinemurian (-200 Ma) Moenave Formation (59.4'N, 59.2'E). Amongst other implica- tions, the sharp change in the APW path at the Jl cusp implies an abrupt change from counterclock- wise rotation of Pangea prior to

riassic-Early Jurassic por- tion of the North American APW path. Furthermore, these data support the geometry of the Jl cusp predicted by the PEP model and provide further constraints for geologic interpreta- tions based on Mesozoic paleomagnetism. D. Elmore School of Geology and Geophysics, University of Oklahoma, Norman Abstract. An early, synsedimentary, chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) is found in and below terra rosa paleosols which cap regressive carbonate cycles in the Pennsylvanian (Morrowan) Black Prince Limestone in southeastern Arizona. Authigenic hematite, occurring in fractures between soil nodules, in Liesegang bands, and replacing allochems, is abundant in specific horizons and is related to soil-formi

ated to soil-forming processes. Paleomagnetic analysis of many specimens from the paleosol horizons reveals both northwesterly and shallow and southeasterly and shallow directions. These unidirectional, northwesterly and southeasterly magnetizations are interpreted to be antipodal equivalents and show a stratigraphic distribution with at least three reversals. The latter two species suggest a Barremian age (J. F. Babinot, personal communication, 1989). Stratigraphically, the Hutubi Formation is part of the Tugulu Group, which according to Chen [1983] spans the entire early Cretaceous. The Hutubi Formation is overlain by the Shengjinkou Formation, itself overlain by the Lianmuqin Formation. In Wuerhe district, in the northwestern part of the Dzungar Basin, the Lianmuqin Formation has yielded a fairly varied vertebrate fauna [Dong, 1973] containing, among others, the dinosaur Psittacosaurus. Psittacosaurus is known in several other localities in Asia, from Siberia and Mongolia to northern China and Thailand [Buffetaut et al., 1989], in rocks which seem to correspond to the later part of the early Cretaceous (Aptian/Albian). The older Hutubi Formation is thus probably pre-Aptian in age. The strata outcrop on steeply dipping (>50 ø ) limbs of anticlines with roughly east-west fold axes (Figures. 2 and 3). Indeed, we must address the question of whether these directions have suffered from compaction-induced inclination shallowing before the paleomagnetic inclinations can be interpreted in terms of paleolatitudes. This problem has recently been analyzed for natural sediments [Arason and Levi, 1990a], redeposited sediments [Levi and Banerjee, 1990], synthetic sediments [Dearner and Kodarna, 1990] or by numerical modeling [Arason and Levi, 1990b]. The present approach should give a better knowledge not only of the Mesozoic evolution of the Bay of Biscay but also of the regions around the Iberian Peninsula. We carefully selected the region and the sedimentary series to be sampled. A major requirement was to sample well dated rocks in a tectonically stable region of Iberia far away from the Pyrenean and the Betic chains. The Lisboa region seems to fulfill a lot of these requirements (Fig. 1). It has been slightly de- formed during the rifting phases between the Iberian and North American plates, mainly before Early Cretaceous. Some deformation occurred also during the emplacement of the intrusive Sintra Massif, and the Tertiary. Sedimentary facies of outer platform prevailed before the late Bar- remian. The lithologic and stratigraphic succession is particularly well known [17]. The present approach should give a better knowledge not only of the Mesozoic evolution of the Bay of Biscay but also of the regions around the Iberian Peninsula. We carefully selected the region and the sedimentary series to be sampled. A major requirement was to sample well dated rocks in a tectonically stable region of Iberia far away from the Pyrenean and the Betic chains. The Lisboa region seems to fulfill a lot of these requirements (Fig. 1). It has been slightly de- formed during the rifting phases between the Iberian and North American plates, mainly before Early Cretaceous. Some deformation occurred also during the emplacement of the intrusive Sintra Massif, and the Tertiary. Sedimentary facies of outer platform prevailed before the late Bar- remian. The lithologic and stratigraphic succession is particularly well known [17]. Furthermore, be- cause of the high density of population, building activity and quarries provided us with numerous fresh outcrops. 2. The present approach should give a better knowledge not only of the Mesozoic evolution of the Bay of Biscay but also of the regions around the Iberian Peninsula. We carefully selected the region and the sedimentary series to be sampled. A major requirement was to sample well dated rocks in a tectonically stable region of Iberia far away from the Pyrenean and the Betic chains. The Lisboa region seems to fulfill a lot of these requirements (Fig. 1). It has been slightly de- formed during the rifting phases between the Iberian and North American plates, mainly before Early Cretaceous. Some deformation occurred also during the emplacement of the intrusive Sintra Massif, and the Tertiary. Sedimentary facies of outer platform prevailed before the late Bar- remian. The lithologic and stratigraphic succession is particularly well known [17]. Furthermore, be- cause of the high density of population, building activity and quarries provided us with numerous fresh outcrops. 2. The present approach should give a better knowledge not only of the Mesozoic evolution of the Bay of Biscay but also of the regions around the Iberian Peninsula. We carefully selected the region and the sedimentary series to be sampled. A major requirement was to sample well dated rocks in a tectonically stable region of Iberia far away from the Pyrenean and the Betic chains. The Lisboa region seems to fulfill a lot of these requirements (Fig. 1). It has been slightly de- formed during the rifting phases between the Iberian and North American plates, mainly before Early Cretaceous. Some deformation occurred also during the emplacement of the intrusive Sintra Massif, and the Tertiary. Sedimentary facies of outer platform prevailed before the late Bar- remian. The lithologic and stratigraphic succession is particularly well known [17]. Furthermore, be- cause of the high density of population, building activity and quarries provided us with numerous fresh outcrops. 2.
